newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Powerful Philippine church opposes 2nd Ramos term.
newsitem.headline: Powerful Philippine church opposes 2nd Ramos term.

text.p: The Philippines' powerful Roman Catholic Church on Sunday attacked moves to extend President Fidel Ramos's term in office, warning it could provoke street demonstrations, endanger the economy and destabilise the nation.

In a letter read in churches nationwide, the country's more than 100 Catholic bishops opposed the calling of a plebiscite to allow Ramos to run for re-election, and said an extended Ramos term had raised popular fears of a return of authoritarian rule.

"Have we become so poor and so dependent on one man that we can no longer continue with our progress unless he remains as president?" asked the letter issued by the Catholic Bishops Conference of the Philippines.
The constitution, in reaction to the late Ferdinand Marcos's 20-year rule, limits a president to only one term of six years.
Ramos, elected in 1992, has repeatedly said he will step down when his term ends in June 1998.

But several citizens groups, reportedly backed by some presidential aides, have been campaigning to collect five million signatures to force the calling of a plebiscite that would either lift Ramos's term limit or allow him to run for a second term.
They said Ramos deserved a second term to ensure continuity of his reform program that had turned the economy around.
"The pursuit of charter changes at this time...will only generate more politicaly destabilising argumentation, debate and demonstrations," the church's letter said.
Changing the charter now would have "grave adverse effects on our political and economic situation," the letter added.
It urged Filipinos to unite in opposing any charter change, saying that "will seriously endanger our nation's gains".
In the only instance when a Philippine president was elected to a second term, he stayed in power for 20 years and had to be ousted in a 1986 popular revolt, it added, referring to Marcos.
"We must be wise as serpents," the letter said, warning against wolves who might come "in sheep's clothing".

The Supreme Court last month virtually killed the signature campaign by saying there was no law providing for the staging of a plebiscite to amend the charter. Amendment supporters have appealed the verdict and have been plastering city walls with signs reading: "Let the people decide."
